extracted.intended_audience: readers and scholars of English social/cultural history and popular entertainments (16th–17th century)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted procedural and practical standards, licensing rules, and performance practices governing strolling players, showmen, and fair entertainments in 16th–17th century England as described in a historical chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annual licence duty to the Master of the Revels
rubrics_metrics.description: All these professors of the various arts of popular entertainment had, at this period, to pay an annual licence duty to the Master of the Revels, whose office was created by Henry VIII. in 1546.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The office's jurisdiction extended over all wandering minstrels and every one who blew a trumpet publicly, except 'the King's players.' The seal and legend of the office were used under five sovereigns. (Context: the licence duty functioned as a formal regulatory mechanism controlling itinerant entertainers.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal classification under the Vagrancy Act (Elizabethan) of jugglers and minstrels
rubrics_metrics.description: The Vagrancy Act of Elizabeth's reign scheduled jugglers and minstrels with strolling thieves, gipsy fortune-tellers, and itinerant beggars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This classification subjected entertainers to penalties and social stigma; it drew a broad legal line between acceptable amusements for the upper classes and those for the masses. (Context: this statutory categorization limited entertainers' rights and was invoked in later enforcement.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppression and penalties under Puritan/Parliamentary rule (1647 onward)
rubrics_metrics.description: In 1647 the entertainers of the people were forbidden to exercise their vocation, the theatres were closed, the May-poles removed, and the fairs shorn of all their wonted amusements, and reduced to the status of annual markets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforcement included whipping, imprisonment, and other punishments (actors and showmen faced Bridewell, the whipping-post, and imprisonment as 'idle vagabonds'). Performances continued only covertly or by bribing officials when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing requirement for ballad-singers and suppression of unlicensed performers (post-Restoration practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ballad-singers and vendors were required to take out licences at the office of the revels, at Whitehall, for singing and selling of ballads and small books, according to an ancient custom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Announcements (1682) directed ballad-singers to obtain licenses and warned that mountebanks, rope-dancers, prize-players, ballad-singers, and such as made shows of strange sights without a license in red and black letters under the hand and seal of the Master of the Revels would be suppressed. The licensing function could be leased (e.g., to a bookseller) and was enforced by civic authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy by noble patronage for acting companies
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies that had permission to call themselves by the name of some nobleman and to wear his livery (e.g., 'my Lord Leicester's company') were distinguished from unlicensed or unrecognised strolling players.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affiliation with a noble patron conferred recognized status and allowed such companies to perform in places where unlicensed troupes could not; it functioned as a form of authorization and protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of pictorial advertising outside shows
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of displaying in front of the shows large pictures of the wonderful feats, or curious natural objects, to be seen within, prevailed in the sixteenth century, and probably long before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literary allusions (e.g., Jonson's The Alchymist) cite 'banners / Of a strange calf with five legs to be seen' as evidence that pictorial signage was used to draw and instruct potential patrons about the attractions inside. (Implication: visual advertising was a standard method of audience attraction.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Illusion staging and misdirection practices (example: decollation/decapitation trick)
rubrics_metrics.description: The decollation trick ('decollation of St. John the Baptist') was performed upon a table with a dish to receive the head; the table had two holes (one to enable the assistant to conceal his head, the other to receive the head of another confederate concealed beneath the table); the knife had a semi-circular opening in the blade to fit the neck; an ordinary knife was shown and then surreptitiously substituted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The trick relied on specially contrived props (table and dish with holes), concealed assistants, a specially shaped implement, and sleight-of-hand substitution to misdirect spectators. (Implication: successful stage illusions required careful prop construction and practiced misdirection.)
